The cursor blinks. It is a tiny, persistent pulse of light against a void of white, demanding something from nothing. One thousand words. It sounds like a lot until you start typing, and then it feels like an ocean, and you are standing at the shore with a teaspoon. 

Where do thoughts go before they become words? They live in a strange, pre-linguistic soup of emotion, sensation, and abstract imagery. I feel the caffeine from my second cup of coffee vibrating slightly in my fingers. I hear the low, rhythmic hum of the refrigerator in the next room, a modern-day hearth keeping things from spoiling. Outside, the world is moving—cars swishing on wet asphalt, the distant, muffled bark of a neighbor's dog, the wind shaking the last stubborn leaves from the oak tree by the driveway. 

Autumn is a season of transition, but it feels more like a finale. The trees are stripping themselves bare, unapologetic in their vulnerability. They don't hoard their energy; they let go. There is a lesson in that, whispered every October and November, though we humans are terrible at listening to it. We hold onto everything. We hold onto old grudges, embarrassing moments from 2012, expired cans of soup in the back of the pantry, and expectations of who we were supposed to be by now.

If I could write about anything, why do I write about time? Probably because it’s the only currency we all spend at the exact same rate, yet we act like some of us have vaults of it hidden away. Every keystroke is a micro-second vanishing into the ether. Click, clack, tap. The mechanical keyboard offers a satisfying tactile feedback, a reminder that physical actions still matter in a world that is increasingly intangible. We live in the cloud, we store our memories in silicon chips, we converse with glowing rectangles, but the desire to leave a mark—to push ink onto paper or pixels onto a screen—remains stubbornly ancient.

Think about the first person who painted a hand stencil on a cave wall in Altamira or Lascaux. They blew pigment around their hand, leaving a negative space that says, *I was here.* They didn't have Wi-Fi. They didn't have retirement accounts or existential dread about the housing market. They had predators, berries, cold nights, and the crushing, beautiful weight of consciousness. They looked at the dark rock and felt the urge to say, *Look. I existed.*

That is what writing is, really. It’s a hand pressed against a cave wall. 

I wonder who will read this, or if anyone ever will. Maybe it’s just for the algorithm, feeding the hungry machine that processes human utterance and turns it into patterns. Maybe it’s for me, a way to untangle the knotted Christmas lights of my brain on a Tuesday afternoon. Does it matter? The act of creation has its own internal gravity. Once you start pulling the thread, the whole sweater starts to unravel, and you just have to keep pulling and see what shape emerges.

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about smallness. We spend so much of our lives trying to be big—trying to make an impact, to leave a legacy, to be important. We want our names remembered. But the universe is unfathomably vast, stretching out in all directions with a cold, silent indifference that should terrify us, but instead, if you look at it right, is deeply comforting. 

You are a temporary arrangement of stardust. The atoms currently making up your left pinky finger were once forged in the heart of a dying star billions of years ago. You are the universe waking up for a brief, shining moment, looking around in bewilderment, and asking, *What is going on here?* And then, just as quickly, you scatter back into the dark, your atoms repurposed to build grass, or rain, or the wing of a beetle. 

Knowing that makes failure feel remarkably low-stakes. If you mess up a presentation, if you say the wrong thing at a dinner party, if your novel gets rejected, if you burn the toast—does it echo across the cosmos? Not even a little bit. The Andromeda galaxy is hurtling toward us at 110 kilometers per second, completely unbothered by your awkward social interaction. 

So why not be bold? Why not say the weird thing, write the messy story, love the person, take the trip, plant the garden? We treat life like a dress rehearsal for a show that never actually opens. We wait for the "right time" to start living, as if time is something we own rather than something that consumes us. 

I look back at the word count. I am perhaps a third of the way there. It is strange how the mind starts to flag, how the well begins to draw up mud instead of water after just a few paragraphs. Writing is a muscle, and mine is cramping. But that’s the beauty of this prompt—it doesn’t require perfection, only endurance. Just keep moving the fingers. Let the grammar be slightly jagged. Let the thoughts wander down alleys they shouldn't. 

There is freedom in incoherence. We are so obsessed with curation. Instagram feeds are color-coordinated; resumes are polished until they reflect a fictional perfection; opinions are focus-grouped and sanitized for public consumption. Nobody wants to see the messy draft. Nobody wants to watch the sausage being made. But the mess is where the life is. The messy draft has crossed-out lines, misspelled words, sudden changes of heart, and abrupt endings. The messy draft is honest.

If I could give my younger self a piece of advice, it wouldn't be about finance, or career choices, or relationships. It would simply be: *Relax. You are taking all of this way too seriously.* 

We walk around with our shoulders hiked up to our ears, jaw clenched, bracing for impact, as if life is an obstacle course designed to trip us up. And sometimes it is. Sometimes it’s brutally unfair. Terrible things happen to wonderful people for no discernible reason. The universe doesn't hand out gold stars for suffering, and karma isn't a cosmic accountant keeping a ledger. Pain just happens, random and indiscriminate as a summer thunderstorm.

Yet, joy happens just as randomly. A stranger smiles at you in line at the grocery store. The sun breaks through the clouds right as you step outside. A song you haven’t heard in ten years comes on the radio, and suddenly you are nineteen again, driving down a back road with the windows down, feeling invincible and heartbroken all at once. 

We need to make more room for those moments. We need to collect them like sea glass, turning them over in our pockets until the sharp edges are worn smooth. 

The light in the room is shifting now. The afternoon is bleeding into the long, blue shadows of evening. The sky outside the window has turned the color of a bruised plum. Soon, the streetlights will flicker on, casting an orange glow over the damp pavement. People will be coming home from work, kicking off their shoes, turning on stoves, sinking into the quiet relief of their own spaces.

I am running out of things to say, which is the natural fate of any monologue. Eventually, the well goes dry. Eventually, the words stop marching and start sitting down in the road, refusing to go any further. And that is fine. A thousand words is a long way to travel on foot, but we’ve made it. The cursor still blinks, waiting, but the page is full. The void has been pushed back, if only for a little while, with ink and breath and a handful of stardust.
